issues.legal_issue: Delegating the identification of affected areas to the executive is not an excessive delegation when the legislation states its policy and purpose and the identification depends on facts unsuitable for legislative definition.
material_facts: The legislation stated that its purpose was to reclaim and develop land by eradicating the weed from affected areas.
The executive was empowered to identify the affected areas based on the extent and distribution of the weed.
issues.conclusion: The delegation was not excessive because the legislation supplied policy and guidance, while identifying the affected areas was an executive determination of fact.
issues.legal_principle: A legislature may delegate implementation of its stated policy where it supplies adequate guidance; determining which areas meet a factual criterion that is not readily capable of legislative definition may be left to the executive. The Court considered the preamble and long title of the Bhopal Reclamation and Development of Lands (Eradication of Kans) Act, 1954, and section 4(1). It relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_delegation: The proceeding challenges whether legislation has impermissibly delegated legislative power.
predicates.legislation_states_policy: The legislation states the policy and purpose that the delegated power is intended to carry out.
predicates.affected_areas_require_factual_identific: The executive must identify affected areas by assessing facts such as the intensity and distribution of a condition.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a delegation, the delegation is not excessive if the legislation states its policy and the affected areas require factual identification.

issues.legal_issue: A power to include broad areas for property-affecting operations is an unreasonable restriction on the right to hold and enjoy property when interested persons have no opportunity to show that their particular land does not require those operations.
material_facts: Notifications included all villages in several administrative areas, while evidence showed that patches of land in those areas had previously been cleared of the weed.

The law allowed an officer to select land for eradication operations but provided no opportunity for interested persons to object or establish that their land was not infested and did not need treatment.
issues.conclusion: The power to declare areas and select land for operations, without a process for considering objections, was arbitrary and imposed an unreasonable restriction on the right to hold and enjoy property.
issues.legal_principle: Article 19(1)(f) protected the right to hold and enjoy property. Sections 4(1) and 4(4), read together and in the absence of a procedure for objections, imposed an unreasonable restriction in the circumstances, including evidence of cleared patches within the notified areas. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_res: The proceeding challenges a law that restricts the holding or enjoyment of property.
predicates.no_objection_process: The law provides no opportunity for interested persons to establish that their particular land does not require the proposed operations.
predicates.affected_area_contains_land_not_requirin: Evidence shows that an area included in a notification contains land that does not require the proposed operations.

issues.definition: A property restriction is unreasonable when a constitutional challenge concerns it, the law provides no objection process, and the affected area includes land that does not require the operations.

issues.legal_issue: Taking exclusive possession of property without providing compensation is unconstitutional even if the period of possession is short and the owner is exempted from paying land revenue during that period.
material_facts: The law allowed the reclamation authorities to take possession of land and barred the owner from using it until possession was restored by notification.
The law provided no compensation for the taking of possession; exemption from land revenue applied only while the owner could not use the land.
issues.conclusion: The taking of possession without compensation violated Article 31(2), and the exemption from land revenue did not constitute compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31(2), as it stood at the relevant time, required a law authorising the taking of possession of property for public purposes to provide compensation. Sections 4(1), 6(1)(b), and 6(2) established exclusive state possession and prevented the owner from using the land until restoration. The land-revenue exemption in the proviso to section 6(2) merely alleviated the owner's loss and was not compensation; the short duration of possession did not change the character of the taking. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_property_taking and exclusive_state_possession and owner_barred_from_use_until_restoration and no_compensation_for_possession

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_tak: The proceeding challenges a law that authorises the state to take possession of property for public purposes.
predicates.exclusive_state_possession: The state or its officer obtains possession to the exclusion of the owner.
predicates.owner_barred_from_use_until_restoration: The owner is prohibited from using the property until the state restores possession.
predicates.no_compensation_for_possession: The law does not provide compensation for the deprivation of possession.

issues.definition: A taking is unconstitutional when a property-taking challenge involves exclusive state possession, bars the owner from using the property until restoration, and the law provides no compensation for possession.

issues.legal_issue: A contribution demand is unlawful when the required statutory process for calculating and apportioning the costs has not been followed.
material_facts: The law entrusted a board with determining the total expenditure and equitably apportioning it among landholders.
The board never met or made those determinations; instead, the costs and allocations were communicated by the central government and demands were made on that basis.
issues.conclusion: The statutory procedure was mandatory, and because it was not followed, the contribution demands were unlawful and were properly quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 7 and 8 required the prescribed board and officer to determine and apportion costs before a demand could lawfully be made and recovered. The procedure in section 7 was mandatory; a demand could not be made without recourse to that machinery. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.challenge_to_cost_contribution_demand: The proceeding challenges a demand that landholders contribute to the cost of operations on their land.
predicates.statutory_cost_process_requires_authoris: The governing law requires designated bodies or officers to determine the expenditure and apportion it before demanding payment.
predicates.required_process_not_followed: The designated decision-makers did not perform the required cost determination and apportionment before the demand was made.

issues.definition: A contribution demand is unlawful when it is challenged, the governing law requires authorised cost determination and apportionment, and that process was not followed.

issues.legal_issue: A prospective extension of another law cannot validate a demand that was invalid when made.
material_facts: The State relied on legislation extending a different reclamation law to the affected area to support the demands.
That extension operated prospectively, while the demands had already been made and were invalid when made.
issues.conclusion: The extension could not sustain the demands because it operated prospectively and did not validate demands that were invalid when made.
issues.legal_principle: The Madhya Pradesh Reclamation of Lands (Extension to Bhopal) Act, 1957 operated prospectively, not retrospectively. It therefore could not supply a legal basis after the fact for demands that were invalid when issued. The Court relied on no earlier cases for this conclusion.

predicates.appeal_relies_on_later_extension_of_anot: An appeal relies on legislation that later extended a different legal regime to the relevant area.
predicates.extension_operates_prospectively: The extending legislation applies only from its commencement and does not operate retrospectively.
predicates.demand_invalid_when_made: The demand lacked a valid legal basis at the time it was issued.

issues.definition: A prospective extension does not validate a demand when an appeal relies on that extension and the demand was invalid when made.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may decline to consider a quasi-contract ground that was not pleaded or raised in the proceedings below or preserved in the appeal materials.
material_facts: The State sought to rely on a statutory quasi-contract claim for the benefit conferred by operations on the land.
The claim had not been pleaded as a defence in the proceedings below, argued there, or included in the grounds of appeal or the statement of case.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to permit the State to raise the quasi-contract ground at that stage and did not decide whether the claim could otherwise succeed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to entertain the argument based on section 70 of the Indian Contract Act because it had not been pleaded or raised in the proceedings below and had not been included in the appeal grounds or statement of case. The Court made no ruling on the substantive availability of a quasi-contract claim and relied on no earlier cases.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: The court is hearing an appeal from an earlier proceeding.
predicates.new_quasi_contract_ground_not_pleaded_be: A party advances a quasi-contract ground that was not pleaded or argued in the proceeding below.
predicates.ground_not_preserved_in_appeal_materials: The ground was omitted from the appeal grounds and the party's written case on appeal.

issues.definition: A new quasi-contract ground is not considered when it was neither pleaded below nor preserved in the appeal materials.
